title: Philidor gone wrong: which rook squares lose
outcomes: Predicts, for a given rook square, whether the defence still draws or loses
Spots a quick loss: a check along the back rank that wins the defending rook
States that a rook square is checked one position at a time, not by a single rank rule

steps.text: You know the defence from **Philidor: the passive defence that works** and the attacker's goal from *Lucena: building the bridge*. Now see how a wrong rook square costs the game. Some squares lose at once to a skewer: a check along the back rank when your king stands between the two rooks. Look at one, then predict the twin.

steps.caption: Black's rook stands on a8 with the king beside it. White to move wins (tablebase). One line is shown.

line.say: Rook check along the eighth rank. Black's king stands between the two rooks.
The king steps off the rank, so the rook on a8 is attacked.
The pawn gives check and pulls the king away.
White takes the rook on a8 and is a rook up.

steps.text: **When a rook square is wrong.** The attacker gets a check or a skewer, or the king can pass the rook and walk to the pawn. **When it is not wrong.** Many placements still draw. Rule of thumb: ask what the attacker's rook can check, then whether your rook can still reach the sixth rank. Test each placement; do not trust a single-rank rule.
